title: Batch Routine Messages Around Real Response Obligations
subtitle: Protect focused work without hiding time-sensitive channels.
description: Set predictable windows for non-urgent messages, keep an explicit path for work that genuinely cannot wait, and adjust the schedule when it conflicts with actual response duties.
keywords: Cut the Noise with Communication Blocks

lifeOsSource.hack: Batch non-urgent email and chat when your role allows it, while keeping a clear route for work that genuinely cannot wait.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: List the communication channels you monitor, separate channels that require rapid coverage from routine messages, place routine processing into predictable windows, define an exception path for genuinely time-sensitive items, turn longer requests into tasks, and review whether your response obligations are still being met.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Which messages waited until the planned window, which exception was genuinely time-sensitive, and did the schedule still meet the response expectations of my role?

faq.question: What if my role requires fast responses?
faq.answer: Keep the coverage your role actually requires. Apply batching only to channels or message types that can safely wait, and preserve the agreed escalation route for urgent work.

faq.question: How many message windows should I schedule?
faq.answer: There is no fixed number. Start from deadlines, service expectations, collaboration needs, and the amount of routine communication you receive. Adjust the windows when the schedule creates missed obligations or unnecessary switching.

intro.html: Communication batching is a work-design choice, not a rule that everyone should answer messages at the same cadence. The useful version separates routine traffic from genuinely time-sensitive work, gives colleagues a predictable response pattern, and preserves an escalation path when waiting would create a real problem.

sections.title: 1. Map the response obligations
sections.html: List the channels you monitor and the kinds of requests that arrive there. Mark which items have an agreed response target, which can wait until a normal processing window, and which need a clear escalation route. Do not batch work that your role requires you to cover continuously.

sections.title: 2. Set predictable windows for routine traffic
sections.html: Choose message-processing windows that fit the real calendar rather than an idealized schedule. During a window, scan the routine channels, answer short items, and move anything requiring substantial work into the task system with an owner and next action.

sections.title: 3. Define the exception path
sections.html: Decide how genuinely time-sensitive work should reach you outside the routine windows: a designated channel, a call, an agreed escalation tag, or another method already understood by the team. Keep the exception narrow enough that it remains meaningful.

sections.title: 4. Review the operating fit
sections.html: After using the schedule, check for missed commitments, delayed handoffs, duplicated checking, or unnecessary interruptions. Keep the batching pattern when it supports both focused work and response obligations; change it when either side is being damaged.

editorialCuration.reason: Replace unsupported context-switching statistics, invented time-savings, rigid universal message schedules, fabricated observations, and pseudo-optimized block lengths with a role-aware communication batching workflow.
